Calvin Cycle

Calvin Cycle
● The calvin cycle is
  cyclic electron flow
● Uses ATP and NADPH
  to reduce CO2 to sugar
  (G3P)
● For net synthesis of 1
  G3P molecule, the
  cycle must take place 3
  times

Calvin Cycle
Three phases:
1. Carbon fixation
2. Reduction
3. Regeneration of RuBP

Phase 1: Carbon Fixation
● CO2 is incorporated into the calvin cycle one at a
  time
   ○ Each CO2 attaches to a molecule of RuBP
     ■ Catalyzed by the enzyme rubisco
  ○ Forms 3-phosphoglycerate

Phase 2: Reduction
● Each molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate is
  phosphorylated by ATP (uses 6 total)
  ○ Becomes 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate
     ■ 6 NADPH molecules donate electrons to 1,3-
       bisphosphoglycerate
        ● Reduces to G3P
        ● 6 molecules of G3P are formed, but only
          one is counted as a net gain
          ○ The other 5 G3P molecules are used to
             regenerate RuBP

Phase 3: Regeneration of RuBP
● 5 G3P molecules are used to regenerate 3
  molecules of RuBP
  ○ Uses 3 ATP for regeneration
● Cycle is now ready to take in CO2 again

Problem for C3 Plants
Photorespiration:
  ○ On very hot days plants close their stomata to
     stop water loss
  ○ Causes less CO2 to be present, and more O2
  ○ Rubisco binds to O2 and uses ATP
      ■ The process produces CO2
      ■ NO sugar is produced
      ■ BAD for the plant

Adaptations
Plants that live in hot, dry climates have evolved to
have alternative mechanisms of carbon fixation

Adaptations
● C4 Plants
  ○ Spatial separation of steps
  ○ Stomata partially close to
     conserve water
  ○ Mesophyll cells fix CO2 into a
     4-C molecule
    ■ Transferred to bundle
       sheath cells
       ● Releases CO2 to be used
          in the Calvin cycle
  ○ Examples: maize (corn),
    grasses, sugarcane

Adaptations
● CAM plants
  ○ Open stomata at night and close
    during the day
  ○ CO2 is incorporated into organic
    acids and stored in vacuoles
  ○ During the day, light reactions
    occur and CO2 is released from
    the organic acids and
    incorporated into the Calvin cycle
  ○ Examples: pineapples, cacti,
    succulents, jade

was interested in photorespiration. After doing research she claimed that it is
simply a metabolic relic; early atmospheric conditions did not have oxygen,
therefore it never posed a problem early on. Would you support or reject this

There are 2 primary theories. 1) Like stated in the
FRQ, it is a metabolic relic. Early Earth had primarily
only CO2 in the atmosphere, therefore, binding of
oxygen to rubisco was not a problem. 2) Some
theories suggest that photorespiration may protect
plants against harmful products that build up when
the Calvin Cycle is low.

Energy Harvest

  membrane proteins that shuttle electrons down a
  series of redox reactions
  ○ Releases energy used to make ATP
  ○ ETC transfers e- to O2 (the final e- acceptor) to
     make H2O
      ■ Releases energy

2. Pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle
3. Oxidative phosphorylation (ETC and
   chemiosmosis)

ced_current_atoms.label: Enzyme regulation role
ced_current_atoms.statement: Enzyme structure and function contribute to regulation of biological processes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Enzymes are protein catalysts
ced_current_atoms.statement: Enzymes are proteins that function as biological catalysts in cells.

ced_current_atoms.label: Activation-energy reduction
ced_current_atoms.statement: Enzymes facilitate chemical reactions by lowering activation energy.

ced_current_atoms.label: Active-site compatibility
ced_current_atoms.statement: For an enzyme-mediated reaction to occur, substrate shape and charge must be compatible with the enzyme active site.

ced_current_atoms.label: Enzyme-substrate complex
ced_current_atoms.statement: The enzyme-substrate complex model represents substrate binding at the active site.

ced_current_atoms.label: Structure-function disruption
ced_current_atoms.statement: A change to the molecular structure of a component in an enzymatic system may change its function or efficiency.

ced_current_atoms.label: Enzyme denaturation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Temperature, pH, or chemical-environment changes can disrupt enzyme protein structure and eliminate catalytic ability.

ced_current_atoms.label: Temperature and pH outside optimum
ced_current_atoms.statement: Temperatures and pH values outside an enzyme’s optimal range can disrupt interactions that maintain structure and alter catalytic efficiency.

ced_current_atoms.label: Reversible denaturation
ced_current_atoms.statement: In some cases enzyme denaturation is reversible and activity can return when conditions are restored.

ced_current_atoms.label: Substrate and product concentrations
ced_current_atoms.statement: Relative concentrations of substrates and products influence how efficiently an enzymatic reaction proceeds.

ced_current_atoms.label: Temperature and collision frequency
ced_current_atoms.statement: Increasing temperature raises average molecular speed and enzyme-substrate collision frequency until the enzyme’s optimal temperature is reached.

ced_current_atoms.label: Competitive inhibition
ced_current_atoms.statement: Competitive inhibitors can bind reversibly to an enzyme active site and reduce substrate access.

ced_current_atoms.label: Noncompetitive inhibition
ced_current_atoms.statement: Noncompetitive inhibitors can bind allosteric sites and change enzyme activity.

ced_current_atoms.label: Energy input
ced_current_atoms.statement: All living systems require an input of energy.

ced_current_atoms.label: Life and thermodynamics
ced_current_atoms.statement: The high degree of order in living systems is consistent with the first and second laws of thermodynamics.

ced_current_atoms.label: Energy input and maintenance
ced_current_atoms.statement: Energy input must exceed energy loss to maintain biological order and power cellular processes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Energy coupling
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cellular processes that release energy can be coupled to processes that require energy.

ced_current_atoms.label: Loss of energy flow
ced_current_atoms.statement: A significant loss of biological order or energy flow results in death.

ced_current_atoms.label: Sequential metabolic pathways
ced_current_atoms.statement: Energy-related pathways are sequential, allowing controlled transfer of energy through a series of reactions.

ced_current_atoms.label: Pathway intermediates
ced_current_atoms.statement: A product of one reaction in a metabolic pathway commonly serves as a reactant for the next reaction.

ced_current_atoms.label: Conserved core metabolism
ced_current_atoms.statement: Core metabolic pathways such as glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation are conserved across Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya, supporting common ancestry.

ced_current_atoms.label: Photosynthesis overall process
ced_current_atoms.statement: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide, water, and light energy to produce carbohydrates and oxygen.

ced_current_atoms.label: Solar energy capture
ced_current_atoms.statement: Photosynthetic organisms capture solar energy and produce sugars that can be used in biological processes or stored.

ced_current_atoms.label: Prokaryotic origin of photosynthesis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Photosynthesis first evolved in prokaryotic organisms.

ced_current_atoms.label: Atmospheric oxygenation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Scientific evidence supports the claim that cyanobacterial photosynthesis contributed to oxygenation of Earth’s atmosphere.

ced_current_atoms.label: Foundation of eukaryotic photosynthesis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Prokaryotic photosynthetic pathways formed the evolutionary foundation of eukaryotic photosynthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Chloroplast compartments
ced_current_atoms.statement: Stroma and thylakoids are distinct internal regions of chloroplasts.

ced_current_atoms.label: Stroma and carbon fixation
ced_current_atoms.statement: The stroma is the fluid inside the inner chloroplast membrane and outside the thylakoids; Calvin-cycle carbon-fixation reactions occur there.

ced_current_atoms.label: Thylakoid membrane machinery
ced_current_atoms.statement: Thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll organized into photosystems together with electron-transport proteins.

ced_current_atoms.label: Grana and light reactions
ced_current_atoms.statement: Thylakoids form stacks called grana, and the light reactions occur on thylakoid membranes in these stacks.

ced_current_atoms.label: Light-reaction energy products
ced_current_atoms.statement: The light reactions capture light energy to produce ATP and NADPH, which provide energy and reducing power for carbohydrate production in the Calvin cycle.

ced_current_atoms.label: ETC locations across life
ced_current_atoms.statement: Electron transport chain reactions occur in chloroplasts, mitochondria, and across prokaryotic plasma membranes.

ced_current_atoms.label: NADPH formation
ced_current_atoms.statement: In photosynthesis, electrons passing through the thylakoid electron transport system ultimately reduce NADP+ to NADPH in association with photosystem I.

ced_current_atoms.label: Light excitation of chlorophyll
ced_current_atoms.statement: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, raising electrons to higher energy levels in photosystems I and II.

ced_current_atoms.label: Water supplies PSII electrons
ced_current_atoms.statement: Water is split during the light reactions and supplies electrons that replace those lost from photosystem II.

ced_current_atoms.label: Photosystem linkage
ced_current_atoms.statement: Photosystems II and I are embedded in the thylakoid membrane and linked by electron transfer through an electron transport chain.

ced_current_atoms.label: Thylakoid proton gradient
ced_current_atoms.statement: Electron-transfer redox reactions establish an electrochemical proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane, with higher proton concentration in the thylakoid lumen than in the stroma.

ced_current_atoms.label: Photophosphorylation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Protons flow through membrane-bound ATP synthase by chemiosmosis, driving ATP formation from ADP and inorganic phosphate; in photosynthesis this is photophosphorylation.

ced_current_atoms.label: Calvin-cycle energy input
ced_current_atoms.statement: ATP and NADPH generated by the light reactions power carbohydrate production from carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle in the chloroplast stroma.

ced_current_atoms.label: Respiration and ATP synthesis
ced_current_atoms.statement: Cellular respiration uses energy from biological macromolecules to synthesize ATP.

ced_current_atoms.label: Respiration and fermentation across life
ced_current_atoms.statement: Respiration and fermentation are characteristic energy-harvesting processes across forms of life.

ced_current_atoms.label: Aerobic respiration as coordinated pathway
ced_current_atoms.statement: Aerobic cellular respiration in eukaryotes uses coordinated enzyme-catalyzed reactions to capture energy from biological macromolecules.

ced_current_atoms.label: Respiratory electron transfer
ced_current_atoms.statement: NADH and FADH2 deliver electrons to an electron transport chain; in aerobic respiration electrons move toward oxygen as the terminal acceptor, while anaerobic prokaryotes can use other terminal acceptors.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mitochondrial proton gradient
ced_current_atoms.statement: Electron transfer through the respiratory electron transport chain is coupled to formation of a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, with higher proton concentration in the intermembrane space than in the matrix.

ced_current_atoms.label: Cristae and ATP-production surface
ced_current_atoms.statement: Folding of the inner mitochondrial membrane into cristae increases membrane surface area available for electron transport and ATP synthesis.

ced_current_atoms.label: Prokaryotic respiratory membrane
ced_current_atoms.statement: In prokaryotes, electron transport and proton translocation associated with respiration occur across the plasma membrane.

ced_current_atoms.label: Oxidative phosphorylation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Protons flow through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis to drive ATP formation; in aerobic respiration this process is oxidative phosphorylation.

ced_current_atoms.label: Respiratory uncoupling and heat
ced_current_atoms.statement: Decoupling proton flow from ATP production can release stored gradient energy as heat, which can contribute to thermoregulation in endotherms.

ced_current_atoms.label: Glycolysis outputs
ced_current_atoms.statement: Glycolysis releases energy from glucose to form ATP, NADH, and pyruvate.

ced_current_atoms.label: Pyruvate oxidation and Krebs inputs
ced_current_atoms.statement: In eukaryotic aerobic respiration, pyruvate enters mitochondria and oxidation associated with the Krebs cycle transfers electrons to NAD+ and FAD and releases carbon dioxide.

ced_current_atoms.label: Krebs-cycle location and outputs
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, releases carbon dioxide, synthesizes ATP, and transfers electrons to NAD+ and FAD.

ced_current_atoms.label: Reduced coenzymes feed ETC
ced_current_atoms.statement: NADH and FADH2 produced during glycolysis and Krebs-cycle reactions transfer electrons to the inner-membrane electron transport chain.

ced_current_atoms.label: Matrix-intermembrane pH difference
ced_current_atoms.statement: The proton gradient established by respiratory electron transport makes the mitochondrial matrix higher in pH than the intermembrane space.

ced_current_atoms.label: Fermentation and NAD+ recycling
ced_current_atoms.statement: Fermentation allows glycolysis to continue when oxygen is unavailable by regenerating NAD+ and produces reduced organic products such as ethanol or lactate.

review_flags.source_claim: “Organisms obtain energy by breaking the bond between the 2nd and 3rd phosphate.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Breaking a chemical bond requires energy. ATP hydrolysis is exergonic because products are at lower free energy than ATP plus water.
review_flags.resolution: Teach ATP hydrolysis as an overall free-energy-lowering reaction. Preserve slide 19’s correction that usable free energy does not come from bond breaking itself.

review_flags.source_claim: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is presented as course content.
review_flags.why_flagged: The current CED explicitly excludes the Gibbs free-energy equation from AP Exam scope.
review_flags.resolution: Retain free-energy concepts as teacher enrichment and mark the equation as a scope guard, not AP-required recall.

review_flags.source_claim: “Enzyme names end in -ase.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Many enzyme names end in -ase, but important enzymes such as pepsin and trypsin do not.
review_flags.resolution: Use “many enzyme names end in -ase” as a naming convention, not a universal rule.

review_flags.source_claim: Cofactors, coenzymes, and holoenzymes are taught and assessed.
review_flags.why_flagged: These terms are valid biology but are not explicit required knowledge in the current Unit 3 CED.
review_flags.resolution: Keep as teacher-required enrichment because the classroom assessment tests cofactor knowledge.

review_flags.source_claim: Competitive, noncompetitive, reversible, and permanent inhibition are presented as cleanly overlapping categories.
review_flags.why_flagged: Competitive/noncompetitive describe kinetic interaction patterns, while reversible/irreversible describe persistence. Noncompetitive inhibition does not require complete prevention of substrate binding.
review_flags.resolution: Use the CED reversible competitive model for AP scope, describe noncompetitive inhibition as allosteric reduction in activity, and treat irreversible inhibition separately as enrichment.

review_flags.source_claim: “Allosteric activator/inhibitor: substrate binds to allosteric site.”
review_flags.why_flagged: An allosteric activator or inhibitor is a regulatory molecule, not necessarily the enzyme’s substrate.
review_flags.resolution: Replace “substrate” with “regulatory molecule” in the canonical science.

review_flags.source_claim: Detailed allosteric regulation, cooperativity, and feedback inhibition are taught.
review_flags.why_flagged: These are scientifically valid extensions but are more detailed than explicit current CED enzyme requirements.
review_flags.resolution: Keep as teacher-required enrichment; do not label them AP-required solely because they appear in the deck.

review_flags.source_claim: Autotrophs “produce their own food”; heterotrophs “live off other organisms.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The everyday “food” shorthand can blur carbon and energy sources and excludes heterotrophs obtaining organic matter without directly consuming living organisms.
review_flags.resolution: Define autotrophs as building organic molecules from inorganic carbon using an energy source and heterotrophs as obtaining organic carbon from preexisting organic molecules.

review_flags.source_claim: Water is split into “H and O,” and electrons are described as traveling with H+ directly to CO2 to make sugar.
review_flags.why_flagged: Water oxidation supplies electrons to photosystem II and releases protons and O2. Reducing power reaches carbon fixation largely through NADPH rather than direct transfer of hydrogen from water to CO2.
review_flags.resolution: Canonicalize the separate light-reaction and Calvin-cycle roles of water-derived electrons, NADPH, and CO2.

review_flags.source_claim: Detailed visible-light ranges and pigment identities are taught.
review_flags.why_flagged: These details support understanding but exceed explicit current CED naming requirements beyond chlorophyll/photosystems.
review_flags.resolution: Keep wavelength and pigment details as teacher-required enrichment.

review_flags.source_claim: The same electron is described as repeatedly returning to ground state until it reaches P680.
review_flags.why_flagged: Antenna pigments transfer excitation energy among chlorophyll molecules; the reaction-center chlorophyll then donates an excited electron to a primary acceptor.
review_flags.resolution: Represent resonance/excitation-energy transfer separately from electron transfer at the reaction center.

review_flags.source_claim: The “fall” of electrons from PSII to PSI “provides energy to form ATP.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Electron transfer powers proton translocation; ATP synthase uses the resulting proton-motive force to make ATP.
review_flags.resolution: Keep the proton gradient as the explicit energetic intermediary between electron transport and ATP synthesis.

review_flags.source_claim: “The Calvin cycle is cyclic electron flow.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The Calvin cycle is a cyclic carbon-fixation metabolic pathway. Cyclic electron flow is a different light-reaction process around photosystem I.
review_flags.resolution: Rename the Calvin cycle as a cyclic carbon-fixation pathway and never equate it with cyclic electron flow.

review_flags.source_claim: Detailed Calvin-cycle phases, intermediates, enzyme names, and molecule counts are taught and tested.
review_flags.why_flagged: The current CED explicitly excludes memorization of Calvin-cycle steps, molecule structures, and enzyme names apart from ATP synthase.
review_flags.resolution: Keep these details as teacher-required enrichment. AP-required mastery focuses on location, inputs, outputs, and energy relationships.

review_flags.source_claim: P680/P700 and named electron carriers such as plastoquinone, cytochrome, plastocyanin, ferredoxin, and NADP+ reductase are used.
review_flags.why_flagged: The current CED excludes full names of specific ETC carriers and detailed pathway intermediates from AP Exam scope.
review_flags.resolution: Keep named carriers as teacher enrichment or application context, while canonical AP-required records use photosystems, ETC, proton gradient, NADPH, and ATP synthase.

review_flags.source_claim: Closing stomata is summarized as causing “less CO2 and more O2,” and photorespiration is labeled simply “BAD.”
review_flags.why_flagged: CO2 declines and the relative likelihood of rubisco oxygenation rises. Photorespiration lowers net carbon fixation but may also have protective roles under stress.
review_flags.resolution: Teach the tradeoff and avoid an absolute value judgment.

review_flags.source_claim: Early Earth is described as having “primarily only CO2 in the atmosphere.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The early atmosphere had much less free O2 and generally more CO2 than today, but it was not simply an atmosphere of only CO2.
review_flags.resolution: Use the evidence-supported contrast of lower O2 and higher CO2 when rubisco evolved; retain photorespiration’s proposed relic and protective interpretations.

review_flags.source_claim: Photorespiration, C4 photosynthesis, and CAM are taught in detail.
review_flags.why_flagged: These are valid teacher-course extensions but are not explicit required content in the current 2025 Unit 3 CED.
review_flags.resolution: Keep as teacher-required enrichment and do not inflate AP-required scope.

review_flags.source_claim: “Starch is the major source of fuel for animals.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Animals oxidize carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins. There is no universal biologically correct rule that starch is the major fuel for animals, and fats are major long-term energy stores.
review_flags.resolution: Do not canonicalize the claim. Mark TEST-Q016 for revision before reuse and teach glucose/other biological macromolecules as respiratory fuels.

review_flags.source_claim: “If oxygen is present, the pyruvate enters the mitochondria.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Oxygen is not the direct signal that transports pyruvate into mitochondria. In standard aerobic eukaryotic metabolism, pyruvate is transported into mitochondria and oxidized when respiratory metabolism is proceeding.
review_flags.resolution: Qualify the relationship and avoid presenting O2 as the pyruvate transporter trigger.

review_flags.source_claim: “Each oxygen pairs with 2 H+ and 2 e− to form H2O.”
review_flags.why_flagged: The statement is ambiguous between an oxygen atom and O2. The balanced terminal reaction is O2 + 4 e− + 4 H+ → 2 H2O.
review_flags.resolution: Use the balanced relationship or explicitly say each oxygen atom accepts two electrons and combines with two protons.

review_flags.source_claim: As ETC proteins shuttle electrons, “they also pump H+.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Not every ETC component pumps protons. Specific respiratory complexes couple electron transfer to proton translocation.
review_flags.resolution: Use “certain ETC complexes pump protons” in canonical science.

review_flags.source_claim: Exact stage bookkeeping and ATP yields such as 26–28 and 30–32 ATP per glucose are emphasized.
review_flags.why_flagged: The current CED excludes memorization of detailed steps, enzyme names, and intermediates. Exact ATP yield is model-dependent and not the central required relationship.
review_flags.resolution: Keep exact bookkeeping as teacher enrichment. AP-required mastery emphasizes locations, major inputs/outputs, electron carriers, gradients, and ATP synthase.

review_flags.source_claim: Fermentation is presented as “NO oxygen”; human muscle lactate production is said to occur when muscles “run out of oxygen” and to cause the burning sensation.
review_flags.why_flagged: Fermentation does not require oxygen but can occur even when oxygen is present. Modern physiology does not support lactate as the cause of exercise burning or delayed soreness.
review_flags.resolution: Teach fermentation as NAD+ regeneration that can sustain glycolysis when oxidative metabolism cannot meet demand. Remove the lactate-causes-burning claim and revise TEST-Q023 before reuse.

review_flags.source_claim: Lactate in blood is said to lower pH and lactate buildup is treated as the cause of lactic acidosis.
review_flags.why_flagged: Lactate accumulation is associated with high-rate glycolysis and acid-base disturbance, but lactate itself is not the simple causal acid described by the slide.
review_flags.resolution: Keep lactate shuttling and Cori-cycle concepts as enrichment while avoiding a direct lactate-causes-acidosis mechanism.

review_flags.source_claim: Penicillin is classified as a “competitive inhibitor” that covalently and irreversibly binds transpeptidase.
review_flags.why_flagged: Covalent active-site inhibition is better described as irreversible/mechanism-based inhibition and does not match the standard reversible competitive-inhibition model in the current CED.
review_flags.resolution: Retain the scenario as teacher enrichment but revise the classification if reused; do not use it to define AP competitive inhibition.

review_flags.source_claim: Bentazon question requires named plastoquinone and cytochrome components.
review_flags.why_flagged: The application is scientifically useful, but the current CED excludes memorization of named ETC carriers.
review_flags.resolution: Keep the scenario as practice-only teacher enrichment and score reasoning about electron flow, proton gradient, ATP/NADPH, and photosynthetic disruption.

review_flags.source_claim: The teacher deck uses a legacy seven-topic Unit 3 structure.
review_flags.why_flagged: The current Effective Fall 2025 CED has five Unit 3 topics.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve legacy headings as source metadata and map canonical science to current Topics 3.1–3.5.

review_flags.source_claim: The simplified photosynthesis equation displays glucose as the direct carbohydrate product.
review_flags.why_flagged: The Calvin cycle directly yields three-carbon sugar products that can be used to build glucose and other carbohydrates.
review_flags.resolution: Keep the glucose equation as a useful overall simplification, while canonical wording uses carbohydrate production and makes the simplification explicit.

review_flags.source_claim: Anaerobic respiration terminal acceptors are listed as “sulfates or nitrates.”
review_flags.why_flagged: Sulfate and nitrate are examples, not an exhaustive set of non-oxygen terminal electron acceptors.
review_flags.resolution: Present nitrate, sulfate, and other molecules as examples used by different anaerobic organisms.

canonical_catalog.canonical_verified_statement: Metabolism is the complete set of chemical reactions occurring within an organism or cell.
A metabolic pathway is a sequence of enzyme-catalyzed reactions in which intermediates connect an initial substrate to products.
Catabolic pathways break complex molecules into simpler products and typically release usable energy.
Anabolic pathways build complex molecules from simpler components and require energy input.
Energy is the capacity to cause change or perform work in a biological system.
Kinetic energy is energy associated with motion.
Thermal energy is kinetic energy associated with random movement of atoms and molecules.
Potential energy is stored energy associated with position or structure.
Chemical energy is potential energy associated with molecular structure that can be transformed during chemical reactions.
Thermodynamics is the study of energy transformations in matter.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can be transferred or transformed.
Every energy transfer or transformation increases the entropy of the universe, and some energy becomes less available to perform work, often dispersing as heat.
A cell or organism can become more ordered locally while total entropy of the system plus surroundings increases.
Gibbs free energy describes the portion of a system’s energy that can perform work under specified conditions.
The equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS may be used as teacher enrichment, but memorization or use of this equation is beyond the current AP Biology Exam scope.
An exergonic reaction has a negative change in free energy and can proceed spontaneously in the thermodynamic sense; spontaneity does not imply a fast rate.
An endergonic reaction has a positive change in free energy and requires coupling to an energy-releasing process to proceed in cells.
Living cells maintain flows of matter and energy and remain far from equilibrium; reaching equilibrium is incompatible with sustained cellular work.
Mechanical work includes processes such as ciliary movement, chromosome movement, and muscle contraction.
Transport work moves substances across membranes against thermodynamically favored directions.
Chemical work drives endergonic reactions such as synthesis of polymers from monomers.
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is a nucleotide used as an immediate energy-coupling molecule for many forms of cellular work.
ATP contains adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups.
ATP hydrolysis converts ATP and water to ADP and inorganic phosphate and has a negative free-energy change under cellular conditions.
Energy released by ATP hydrolysis comes from the overall chemical change to lower-free-energy products, not from energy released by breaking a phosphate bond itself.
Cells couple exergonic ATP hydrolysis to endergonic cellular processes so the combined process can proceed.
Phosphorylation is transfer or addition of a phosphate group to a molecule; ATP-driven phosphorylation can alter a molecule’s reactivity, free energy, or protein conformation.
ATP is continually regenerated from ADP and inorganic phosphate using energy released by exergonic processes.
Activation energy is the initial energy barrier that reactants must overcome to reach the transition state of a reaction.
A substrate is a reactant molecule on which an enzyme acts.
The active site is the region of an enzyme where compatible substrate binds and catalysis occurs.
Induced fit is a change in enzyme conformation triggered by substrate binding that improves catalytic interactions in the active site.
Enzymes are not consumed by the reactions they catalyze and can participate in repeated reaction cycles.
Many, but not all, enzyme names end in “-ase.”
Enzymes can catalyze reactions involved in catabolic breakdown pathways.
Enzymes can catalyze reactions involved in anabolic biosynthetic pathways.
An enzyme’s optimal temperature and pH are conditions under which its catalytic activity is highest; the optimum differs among enzymes.
At sufficiently high substrate concentration, enzyme active sites can become saturated and reaction rate approaches a maximum for the available enzyme concentration.
A cofactor is a nonprotein helper required for the function of some enzymes; inorganic cofactors can include metal ions.
A coenzyme is an organic cofactor; many coenzymes are derived from vitamins.
A holoenzyme is the catalytically active enzyme complex with its required cofactor or cofactors associated.
Irreversible inhibitors form very stable interactions, often covalent, that persistently inactivate an enzyme; this is distinct from the standard reversible competitive-inhibition model.
For a reversible competitive inhibitor, increasing substrate concentration can reduce the inhibitor’s effect by increasing the probability that substrate occupies the active site.
An allosteric site is a regulatory binding site distinct from an enzyme’s active site.
Allosteric regulation occurs when a regulatory molecule binds noncovalently at a site other than the active site and changes enzyme activity through a conformational change.
An allosteric activator is a regulatory molecule that binds an allosteric site and stabilizes a more active enzyme conformation.
An allosteric inhibitor is a regulatory molecule that binds an allosteric site and stabilizes a less active enzyme conformation.
Cooperativity occurs in some multisubunit enzymes when substrate binding at one active site promotes a conformation that increases activity at other active sites.
Feedback inhibition occurs when a downstream product inhibits an enzyme acting earlier in the same metabolic pathway, reducing further product formation.
Cells regulate metabolic pathways by controlling enzyme activity, enzyme location, and enzyme abundance, including regulation of gene expression.
An autotroph builds organic molecules from inorganic carbon such as CO2 using energy from light or chemical reactions.
A photoautotroph uses light energy to build organic molecules from inorganic carbon.
A heterotroph obtains organic carbon from preexisting organic molecules made by other organisms.
Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes that perform oxygenic photosynthesis; ancient cyanobacterial activity contributed substantially to atmospheric oxygenation.
Leaves are major photosynthetic organs in most plants, with much photosynthesis occurring in mesophyll cells.
Stomata are adjustable epidermal pores that permit CO2 diffusion into leaves and allow O2 and water vapor to diffuse out under typical photosynthetic conditions.
A chloroplast is a photosynthetic organelle bounded by an envelope of two membranes and containing stroma and thylakoids.
Chlorophyll is a photosynthetic pigment embedded in thylakoid membranes that absorbs light used to excite electrons in photosystems.
The common overall equation 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6 O2 is a simplified net model of photosynthesis; the direct carbon-fixation product is not glucose itself.
The O2 released by oxygenic photosynthesis is derived from oxidation of water during the light reactions.
During oxygenic photosynthesis, water is oxidized and carbon dioxide is ultimately reduced to carbohydrate using reducing power carried by NADPH.
Photosynthesis can be organized into light reactions that capture light energy and a Calvin cycle that uses ATP and NADPH to reduce carbon dioxide to carbohydrate.
A photon is a discrete quantum of electromagnetic radiation; photon energy is inversely related to wavelength.
Wavelength is the distance between corresponding points of successive waves; shorter-wavelength photons carry more energy than longer-wavelength photons.
Photosynthetic pigments absorb some wavelengths of visible light and reflect or transmit others; reflected wavelengths contribute to perceived color.
Chlorophyll a is the primary reaction-center pigment in oxygenic photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll b is an accessory chlorophyll that broadens the wavelengths usable for photosynthesis in plants and green algae.
Carotenoids are accessory pigments that broaden light absorption and can dissipate excess light energy, helping protect the photosynthetic apparatus.
A photosystem is a thylakoid-membrane complex containing a reaction center and surrounding light-harvesting pigments and proteins.
A photosystem reaction center contains a special chlorophyll pair and primary electron acceptor where excitation leads to electron transfer.
Light-harvesting complexes contain pigment molecules bound to proteins and transfer excitation energy toward the reaction center.
Photosystem II absorbs light, transfers an excited electron to an acceptor, and receives replacement electrons from water oxidation.
Photosystem I re-excites electrons arriving from the thylakoid electron transport chain and supports reduction of NADP+ to NADPH.
P680 and P700 are conventional labels for the reaction-center chlorophyll pairs of photosystem II and photosystem I, named for characteristic absorption peaks.
Specific carrier names such as plastoquinone, cytochrome complexes, plastocyanin, ferredoxin, and NADP+ reductase may be used as teacher context but are beyond required AP Exam memorization.
Oxidation of water associated with photosystem II supplies electrons, releases protons into the thylakoid lumen, and produces molecular oxygen.

In light-harvesting complexes, excitation energy is transferred among pigment molecules until reaction-center chlorophyll is excited; the same electron is not passed from antenna pigment to antenna pigment.
The light reactions use light, water, ADP plus inorganic phosphate, and NADP+ and produce O2, ATP, and NADPH.
The Calvin cycle is a cyclic carbon-fixation pathway in the chloroplast stroma that uses ATP and NADPH to incorporate CO2 into carbohydrate.
Carbon fixation is incorporation of inorganic CO2 into an organic molecule; in the Calvin cycle CO2 is added to a carbon acceptor.
Rubisco is the enzyme that catalyzes the initial CO2-fixation reaction of the Calvin cycle and can also react with O2.
Ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) is the CO2-acceptor molecule regenerated in the Calvin cycle.
Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P) is a three-carbon sugar produced by the Calvin cycle and can be used to synthesize glucose and other organic molecules.
For the teacher-taught three-CO2 accounting model, three turns consume 9 ATP and 6 NADPH, produce one net G3P, and use five additional G3P equivalents to regenerate three RuBP.
Memorization of Calvin-cycle steps, intermediate structures, and enzyme names other than ATP synthase is beyond the current AP Exam scope.
Photorespiration occurs when rubisco reacts with O2 instead of CO2, consuming energy and lowering net carbon fixation; it is favored when internal CO2 is low relative to O2.
One hypothesis treats photorespiration as an evolutionary legacy from lower-O2, higher-CO2 conditions; evidence also suggests possible protective roles when the Calvin cycle is limited.
C4 plants initially fix CO2 into four-carbon compounds in mesophyll cells and deliver concentrated CO2 to bundle-sheath cells, reducing photorespiration through spatial separation.
CAM plants open stomata mainly at night, store fixed carbon in organic acids, and release CO2 during the day for the Calvin cycle, reducing water loss through temporal separation.
Eukaryotic aerobic respiration uses mitochondrial compartments including the matrix, inner membrane, cristae, and intermembrane space.
A common model for aerobic glucose respiration is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + usable energy captured in ATP plus heat.
Cells can harvest energy from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins; glucose is a central respiratory substrate, but starch is not a universal “major fuel” for animals.
In aerobic respiration, carbon compounds derived from glucose are oxidized and oxygen is reduced as electrons move to lower free-energy states.
NAD+ accepts electrons and a proton to become NADH; NADH carries high-energy electrons to other reactions including the respiratory electron transport chain.
FAD accepts electrons and protons during the citric acid cycle to become FADH2, which can deliver electrons to the respiratory electron transport chain.
A useful eukaryotic model groups aerobic respiration into glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation plus the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules.
In the teacher-taught bookkeeping model, glycolysis invests 2 ATP and produces 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation for a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.
Substrate-level phosphorylation forms ATP by direct enzymatic transfer of a phosphate group from an organic substrate to ADP.
During standard aerobic eukaryotic respiration, pyruvate is transported into mitochondria and oxidized to an acetyl group carried by coenzyme A, producing CO2 and NADH.
Acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) carries a two-carbon acetyl group into the citric acid cycle.
The citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, oxidizes acetyl groups in the mitochondrial matrix and transfers energy to ATP, NADH, and FADH2 while releasing CO2.
In the teacher-taught per-glucose model, two turns of the citric acid cycle yield 4 CO2, 2 ATP, 6 NADH, and 2 FADH2.
Oxidative phosphorylation includes electron transport that establishes a proton gradient and chemiosmosis through ATP synthase.
The respiratory ETC is a series of inner-membrane electron carriers that undergo redox reactions and transfer electrons toward a terminal acceptor.
Energy released by electron transfer through certain ETC complexes is used to pump protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space.
In aerobic respiration, O2 is the terminal electron acceptor and is reduced to water; the balanced terminal reaction is O2 + 4 e− + 4 H+ → 2 H2O.
Chemiosmosis is the use of energy stored in an electrochemical proton gradient as protons move through a membrane-associated process such as ATP synthase.
ATP synthase is a membrane enzyme complex that uses proton-motive force to catalyze formation of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
Proton flow through ATP synthase drives rotational/conformational changes that alter catalytic sites and support ATP formation.

Modern textbook estimates commonly place oxidative phosphorylation near 26–28 ATP and total aerobic yield near 30–32 ATP per glucose in many eukaryotic cells, but exact yield varies with conditions and shuttle costs.
Memorization of detailed glycolysis/Krebs steps, molecular structures, enzyme names, and exact intermediate sequences is beyond the current AP Exam scope.
Anaerobic respiration uses an electron transport chain with a terminal electron acceptor other than oxygen.
Different anaerobic organisms can use terminal electron acceptors such as nitrate, sulfate, or other molecules; nitrate and sulfate are examples, not an exhaustive list.
Fermentation regenerates NAD+ without an electron transport chain so glycolysis can continue when oxidative NADH reoxidation cannot meet demand.
Fermentation does not require oxygen and can support ATP production when oxygen is unavailable, but fermentation pathways can also operate in some cells even when oxygen is present.
Alcohol fermentation converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO2 while oxidizing NADH to regenerate NAD+.
In alcohol fermentation, pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde and acetaldehyde is reduced by NADH to ethanol, regenerating NAD+.
In lactate-producing fermentation, pyruvate is reduced by NADH to lactate, regenerating NAD+.
Human skeletal muscle can produce lactate during high glycolytic flux even when oxygen is present; lactate itself is not the cause of the acute burning sensation or delayed-onset muscle soreness.
Lactate produced by tissues can be oxidized by other tissues or transported to liver and kidney, where its carbon can contribute to glucose synthesis.
